title: The ark (Genesis 6:14–7:24)
hook: a box of wood, pairs of every creature, forty days of rain
tomorrow: the dove and the olive leaf

segments.voice: Yesterday: tzaddik, a righteous person, and the rabbis' argument over whether Noah was good, or good by comparison.

God's instructions to Noah read like a lumber order. Gopher wood. Rooms inside. Pitch, inside and out. Three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, thirty high. Three decks, a window, a door in the side. Then the passengers: a male and a female of every living kind, and of the clean animals, seven and seven, the text says. Food for all of them. Then the fountains of the deep break open, the windows of heaven open, and it rains forty days and forty nights. The water rises above the mountains and stays a hundred and fifty days. Inside, in the dark and the noise: one family and a floating zoo.
screen: `A LUMBER ORDER FROM GOD.` → `EVERY KIND, TWO BY TWO.` → `FORTY DAYS OF RAIN.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew for the ark is tevah, and it doesn't mean a ship. Look at what's missing: no sail, no rudder, no oars, no one steering. A tevah is a box, a chest. It doesn't go anywhere. It floats, and keeps what's inside alive. The word turns up again, in Exodus. A mother hides her baby from Pharaoh's soldiers in a little basket daubed with pitch, and sets it in the reeds by the Nile. That basket is a tevah. The baby is Moses. Two boxes, one enormous and one tiny, both covered with pitch, both steered by no one, both carrying the future of the world on dark water. Why did the building take so long? One midrash says Noah spent a hundred and twenty years on it, planting the trees and cutting them, so that people would ask what he was doing, and have a chance to change. Nobody did. A teaching in the Talmud says his year in the ark was mostly one job: feeding every creature at its own hour, day and night. The hero of the flood spent it hauling food to animals. Later, a Hasidic reading played on tevah also meaning a word: step into the words of your prayer the way Noah stepped into the ark. But the plain story is simpler. When the world is drowning, the task is to carry what's alive.
screen: `TEVAH — A BOX, NOT A SHIP.` · `MOSES' BASKET IS A TEVAH TOO.` · `A HUNDRED AND TWENTY YEARS.` · `A YEAR OF FEEDING.` · then, large: `CARRY WHAT'S ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one living thing that depends on you: a pet, a plant on the windowsill, a child, a parent, a friend in a hard stretch. Picture it clearly, and ask what it needs from you this week: water, a walk, food at the right hour. Nothing heroic; Noah's work was mostly feeding.
The ark. In Hebrew, tevah: a box with no sail and no rudder, built to keep life afloat.
Your line: carry what's alive. Tomorrow, a dove, and what she brings back. Day thirty-three, done.

screen: `DAY 33 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE DOVE AND THE OLIVE LEAF.`

howItsDone: Jews read the flood story in the autumn as part of the weekly Torah portion Noach; Jewish law also counts care for animals, such as feeding them before oneself, as a duty.

original.note: Hebrew: a box or chest. used in the Torah for Noah's ark and for the basket of baby Moses.

trapdoor: what you thought: the ark was a big boat.
what it means: a tevah, a box with no sail or rudder, made to float and keep life alive, not to travel.
what a scholar hears: tevah in Genesis 6–9 and again in Exodus 2:3–5, linking the flood to baby Moses on the Nile.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut the cubit-to-feet conversion and football-field comparison (not in the text); "seven pairs" of clean animals changed to the text's "seven and seven" (pairs vs. individuals is debated); "tevah appears in only one other story" softened to "turns up again, in Exodus" across teach and games.
Cubit conversion removed; the script gives only the text's cubits. 'Seven and seven' (7:2): commentators differ on seven pairs or seven individuals; the script keeps the text's phrase.
Tevah used in the Torah only for Noah's ark and Moses' basket (Exodus 2:3, 2:5): confirm.
Hundred and twenty years of building (Tanhuma Noach 5, cited by Rashi on 6:14; linked to Genesis 6:3): confirm source and that planting the trees is part of the midrash.
Noah feeding the animals at their hours day and night: Sanhedrin 108b. Confirm.
Hasidic reading of tevah as 'word' is attributed to the Baal Shem Tov (Keter Shem Tov and elsewhere); confirm attribution.
Duration aboard about a year (Genesis 7:11 to 8:14): confirm.
howItsDone: feeding animals before oneself (Berakhot 40a, from Deuteronomy 11:15). Confirm.
